candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the text that the host application interpolates (user input, message bodies, configuration/template values, etc.). Everything after the prefix separator is attacker-chosen: in ${script:<engine>:<script>} both the JSR-223 engine name and the script body come from the variable key; in ${url:<charset>:<url>} the charset and URL are attacker-chosen; in ${dns:<op>|<host>} the hostname is attacker-chosen.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: The dangerous lookups are not installed by the plain constructors: new StringSubstitutor()/new StringSubstitutor(Map) leave variableResolver null or map-backed and never add default lookups (StringSubstitutor.java:421-487), so only callers of createInterpolator()/interpolatorStringLookup() with untrusted input are affected. ScriptStringLookup returns null for a null key and wraps lookup failures in IllegalArgumentException, and it requires an engine to be present, so RCE is not universal on modern JDKs without Nashorn/extra engines; however url/dns/file remain exploitable without any engine. The feature is documented in Javadoc, but documentation is not a control and no allow-list, denylist, or opt-in flag exists in this snapshot; the default map is populated unconditionally with all enum entries. No mitigating code path (sandbox, SecurityManager checks) exists in ScriptStringLookup/UrlStringLookup/DnsStringLookup.
candidates.impact: Server-side code execution in the JVM performing substitution when a script engine is available (attacker-supplied script runs with the application's privileges and can perform arbitrary file/network/process actions available to it); server-side request forgery and response disclosure via the url lookup, including non-HTTP protocol handlers supported by the JVM; DNS-based data exfiltration/rebinding-style lookups via the dns lookup; and additional arbitrary file disclosure via the file/xml lookups that are also installed by default. The vulnerability is in a library helper that is explicitly documented for placeholder substitution (StringSubstitutor.java:288-305), so affected callers commonly process externally supplied template text.
candidates.prerequisites: The host application must call StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator(), StringLookupFactory.INSTANCE.interpolatorStringLookup(), or otherwise construct an InterpolatorStringLookup with default lookups, and must pass attacker-influenced text to replace()/lookup(). For code execution, a JSR-223 engine for the requested name must be resolvable (Nashorn 'javascript'/'nashorn' ships with JDK 8-14, the build targets 1.8); without any engine, the url/dns/file lookups still provide SSRF, outbound DNS and file reads. No special permissions beyond the host JVM's are needed.
candidates.root_cause: DefaultStringLookup enumerates DNS, SCRIPT and URL among the default lookups, and StringLookupFactory.addDefaultStringLookups() installs every enum entry into the prefix dispatch map. InterpolatorStringLookup's default constructor enables all of these lookups, and StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator() builds a substitutor over that singleton. Consequently a template substring such as ${script:javascript:...} is dispatched to ScriptStringLookup, which passes the engine name and script body straight from the variable key to ScriptEngineManager.getEngineByName(...).eval(...) with no validation or allow-list. ${url:...} reaches UrlStringLookup's URL.openStream() and ${dns:...} reaches InetAddress.getByName(). The dangerous lookups are therefore active with zero configuration in a documented public helper.
candidates.title: Default interpolation lookups expose script evaluation, URL fetch and DNS resolution to interpolation input
candidates.trace: StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator() (StringSubstitutor.java:303-305) -> StringLookupFactory.interpolatorStringLookup() returns InterpolatorStringLookup.INSTANCE (InterpolatorStringLookup.java:37) -> default constructors flow to InterpolatorStringLookup(map, lookup, true) (lines 58-79, 91-102), which calls StringLookupFactory.addDefaultStringLookups (StringLookupFactory.java:407-416) and inserts every DefaultStringLookup entry, including DNS (line 56), SCRIPT (line 91) and URL (line 101) -> replace() drives substitute() (StringSubstitutor.java:1323-1465) -> resolveVariable() delegates to the lookup (lines 1061-1067) -> InterpolatorStringLookup.lookup() splits at the first ':' and dispatches on the prefix (lines 122-147) -> ${script:...} reaches ScriptStringLookup.lookup(), which splits engine/script and executes new ScriptEngineManager().getEngineByName(engineName).eval(script) (lines 79-86); ${url:...} reaches new URL(urlStr).openStream() (UrlStringLookup.java:73-85); ${dns:...} reaches InetAddress.getByName(subValue) (DnsStringLookup.java:84-99).
candidates.unverified: No build or runtime execution was performed; the exact engine set on a given JVM/classpath and the specific downstream callers that pass untrusted text were not enumerated. Whether http/file protocol handlers are enabled for the JVM (affecting url-lookup file reads) was not tested, and the XML lookup's parser configuration (possible XXE via ${xml:...}) was not analyzed in depth.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-94/CWE-95 (code injection via dynamic evaluation), CWE-918 (SSRF); attacker-controlled interpolation keys reach sensitive operations

coverage_summary: Scope: all 125 visible files under the assigned source root (Apache Commons Text 1.9; src/main/java plus site/build metadata; no test sources are present in the snapshot; no binary files were skipped). I read the entire lookup package (DefaultStringLookup, StringLookupFactory registration paths, InterpolatorStringLookup, ScriptStringLookup, DnsStringLookup, UrlStringLookup, FileStringLookup, PropertiesStringLookup, ResourceBundleStringLookup, XmlStringLookup, ConstantStringLookup, AbstractStringLookup), the core substitution engine of StringSubstitutor (constructors, createInterpolator, resolveVariable, substitute, cyclic handling), StringSubstitutorReader, the translate package unescapers (NumericEntityUnescaper, OctalUnescaper, StringEscapeUtils CSV/HTML paths), RandomStringGenerator, and the CI/pom configuration. I also ran repository-wide searches for process execution, reflection, deserialization, URL opening, and regex compilation sinks to look for stronger injected issues; none were found.
limitations: Static review only: no compilation, tests, or runtime execution were performed, so exploitability statements are based on source semantics, not observed behavior.

No upstream baseline/diff was available, so subtle injected mutations cannot be entirely ruled out; however the reviewed modules are internally consistent with the 1.9 design and the candidate behavior is explicit in the source.

Script-engine availability (e.g. Nashorn on JDK 8-14 vs. removed on later JDKs) and the exact set of downstream callers that feed untrusted text to createInterpolator() are environment-specific and were not enumerated.
XML lookup parser hardening (XXE) was not fully analyzed, and no test sources were available to corroborate behavior.
Coverage is limited to the assigned snapshot; generated/compiled artifacts and external dependencies (commons-lang3, checkstyle, etc.) were not inspected.

rejected_leads.lead: XmlStringLookup performs XPath evaluation over an attacker-named file (${xml:path:xpath}) with XPathFactory.newInstance().newXPath().evaluate(xpath, new InputSource(inputStream)), which can read arbitrary files and may allow external-entity/XXE behavior depending on the JAXP parser defaults.
rejected_leads.reason: It is a consequence of the same root cause (powerful lookups installed by default) and the XXE part depends on unspecified JAXP defaults; lower direct evidence of independent, concrete impact than the script/url lookups, so it was folded into the main candidate rather than scored separately.

rejected_leads.lead: NumericEntityUnescaper writes Character.toChars(entityValue) for any entityValue > 0xFFFF; values above Character.MAX_CODE_POINT (e.g. �) make Character.toChars throw an unchecked IllegalArgumentException while unescaping HTML/XML input.
rejected_leads.reason: Appears to be the upstream 1.9 behavior, is at most a per-call unchecked-exception/availability issue, and lacks evidence of a stronger security impact; not selected.

rejected_leads.lead: UrlStringLookup opens arbitrary URLs (including non-HTTP protocol handlers) and returns the body; FileStringLookup reads arbitrary paths.
rejected_leads.reason: Both are impacts of the same default-lookup root cause rather than distinct root causes, so they are reported as part of the single candidate instead of separate findings.

rejected_leads.lead: RandomStringGenerator uses ThreadLocalRandom rather than a cryptographic source.
rejected_leads.reason: Documented design for a general-purpose random string utility, not presented as a security-sensitive generator; no security claim or secret-generation use case is made in the class.

summary: Reviewed the 125-file snapshot (Apache Commons Text 1.9 main sources; no test sources present). The strongest, best-evidenced issue is the unsafe default set of interpolation lookups wired into the public helper StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator(): the default lookup map includes the 'script', 'dns' and 'url' lookups in addition to 'file'/'xml'. Any application that runs attacker-influenced text through this interpolator allows server-side script evaluation (RCE where a JSR-223 engine such as Nashorn is present), URL fetch/SSRF, DNS-based exfiltration and file reads, depending only on the prefixes the attacker embeds (e.g. ${script:...}). This is the well-known unsafe-by-default string-substitution design (CVE-2022-42889 class) present in this version; the snapshot contains no allow-list, opt-out, or restriction around these lookups.
